endorsements.quote: Institutions could establish Ethics and Society Review boards, like Stanford Health’s, to examine the societal impacts of AI projects 58 .
AI vendors should be required to provide training on AI bias and algorithmic robustness to enable users to critically evaluate these technologies.
Additionally, patients and providers must be educated on safely interacting with AI, with an option to opt out of AI use when transparency around algorithm development and validation is lacking.
To address these challenges and protect both clinician and patient data, robust access controls, audit trails 42 , transparency standards, and encryption measures are necessary 49 .

unlisted_practices: Healthcare institutions should demand clear protocols and comprehensive disclosures from AI developers and EHR vendors detailing when, where, how, and why AI is used, along with the specific features involved.
Clinicians should champion the development of local AI governance frameworks that ensure AI systems are deployed safely and equitably.
Establish multi-stakeholder assessment and review of AI algorithms both before and after deployment, engaging clinicians, ethicists, patients, and caregivers.
Give providers transparency into monitoring practices and disclosure management systems that let them opt in or out of monitoring where possible.
Collaborate across vendors, institutions, IRBs, government agencies, patient advocacy groups, and licensing organizations to run large-scale AI literacy education for the public and clinicians.
Regulatory bodies should oversee the deployment of LLMs to ensure fair and unbiased application.
Distribute liability for AI-driven decisions appropriately among developers, institutions, and clinicians rather than placing it disproportionately on clinicians.

screen.reason: This is a perspective/commentary article discussing the ethical, legal, and operational governance concerns (transparency, accountability, oversight) of integrating LLMs into electronic health records.
